system:
You split the story sections of one division of a prose work into moments for an illustration engine, which draws one picture per moment.

The text comes as numbered paragraphs: each line starts with its id in square brackets and its word count in parentheses, for example `[12] (34w)`. After the text you get the division's story sections, each with its first and last paragraph id.

Return moments, in order. A moment is a run of consecutive paragraphs that is one beat you can picture: one place, one continuous action or exchange, seen at one instant. Aim for roughly 100 to 400 words per moment, using the word counts given; a moment may be shorter when the beat is a single striking paragraph, and may run past 400 only when one unbroken exchange cannot be cut. Very short paragraphs (lines of dialogue) join their neighbours. Moments tile every section: each paragraph belongs to exactly one moment, moments never cross a section boundary, and together they cover every paragraph of every section with no gaps and no overlaps. Give each moment its first and last paragraph id, the section it lies in (by its first paragraph id), and a one-line summary of what you would see in the picture: who is there, where, doing what. Do not quote the text.

moments.summary: Holmes in his Baker Street sitting-room, tossing aside a newspaper and gesturing with his cherry-wood pipe as he lectures Watson beside the fire.
Watson and Holmes exchanging sharp words across the hearth, Holmes leaning back with pipe in hand while Watson sits stiffly, both in the morning fog-lit room.
Holmes slumped in his chair with a crumpled letter tossed to Watson, the gas-lit breakfast table still uncleared and fog pressing at the windows.
Watson reads the short letter from Violet Hunter while Holmes glances at the clock, the two men by the fire as the expected visitor's ring sounds.
A brisk, freckled young woman enters Baker Street and takes a seat, Holmes rising to greet her as she prepares to recount her story.
Violet describes the stout, smiling Mr. Westaway's office at the agency, a prodigiously stout man with a rolling chin studying her across the desk from Miss Stoper.
The stout employer in the agency office produces a banknote while questioning Violet with a broad smile, Miss Stoper watching from her ledgers.
Violet recounts the agency scene: the stout man rolling his fat hands as he speaks, Miss Stoper's annoyed face as she strikes the gong to dismiss her.
Violet at her lodgings reading aloud Rucastle's letter by lamplight, her bills and meagre cupboard visible on the table.
Holmes and Violet by the Baker Street fire as she states her resolve, Holmes leaning forward with steepled fingers while Watson listens nearby.
Holmes urging caution to Violet at the door, the two of them in the lamp-lit room as she prepares to leave and Watson watches her descend the stairs.
Holmes and Watson in the Baker Street sitting-room over a fortnight, Holmes brooding in his armchair, then at night the telegram handed across to Watson.
Holmes bent over his retort and test-tube at night while Watson studies the Bradshaw timetable, the two men preparing to travel.
Watson and Holmes in a railway carriage, Holmes with the newspapers thrown down, gazing out at the spring countryside of the Hampshire hills.
Holmes and Watson speaking in the train compartment as they pass lonely farmhouses, Holmes gesturing toward the isolated homesteads.
Violet waiting in a private sitting-room at the Black Swan Hotel in Winchester, the lunch laid on the table as the two men enter.
Violet at the Black Swan table describing the Copper Beeches house and its setting to Holmes, who sits with long legs stretched toward the fire.
Violet recounting the Rucastle household to Holmes in the hotel sitting-room, describing the pale wife and the spoiled child she has observed.
Violet in the Copper Beeches drawing-room in the blue dress, seated in the window chair while Rucastle tells comic stories and Mrs. Rucastle sits sadly.
Violet glancing into a hand-mirror at a bearded man in grey by the Southampton road while Mrs. Rucastle stands and draws the blind down.
Violet at the outhouse door at Copper Beeches as Rucastle shows her the slit in the planks and the great tawny mastiff in the gloom beyond.
Violet alone in her bedroom at the chest of drawers, holding up her own coil of hair as she stands by the open drawer.
Rucastle emerging red-faced and furious from the locked wing with keys in hand, Violet watching from the stair.
Rucastle and Violet on the lawn beside the shuttered windows, the photography remark exchanged, then Violet at the bolted door of the forbidden passage.
Violet in a stone corridor pressed against Rucastle at the barricaded door, his face twisted in a demon's grin as he threatens her, then she flees to her room.
Holmes pacing Violet's room with hands in pockets, questioning her about Toller and the cellar as she listens intently.
Holmes in a lamp-lit room explaining the deduction to Violet and Watson, gesturing as he reasons about the child's cruelty.
Violet standing smiling at the door-step of Copper Beeches at sunset under the dark copper trees while Holmes and Watson arrive.
Holmes, Watson and Violet in the bare passage before the barricaded door, Watson braced against the old rickety door as it gives way into the empty room.
Holmes swinging himself up through the open skylight onto the roof while Violet and Watson watch from the empty room below, the light ladder against the eaves.
A burly, fat man with a heavy stick confronts Holmes in the doorway as Violet shrinks against the wall, Holmes shouting at him before he turns and runs down the stairs.
Holmes, Watson and Toller rushing round the side of the house, where the mastiff has Rucastle pinned on the lawn and Watson fires his revolver.
Mrs. Toller standing in the drawing-room doorway as Violet gasps at her, the tall gaunt woman speaking as the others turn toward her.
Holmes seated opposite Mrs. Toller in the drawing-room, listening with a keen look while she explains Alice's history and Fowler's role.
Holmes, Watson and Violet in the drawing-room as the surgeon and Mrs. Rucastle arrive, Holmes gathering his coat to leave the house.
